items.question: What lies beyond the salt ocean and which mountains stand to its north?
premises: The salt ocean measures one hundred thousand yojanas.
Outside that salt ocean there are mountains.
To the north stand the mountains Rishabha, Dundubhi, Dhumra, Kanka, Drona, and Indu.
items.inference: The salt ocean is bounded on its northern side by a specific group of named mountains.
uncertainties: The exact compound split of puro@drayaḥ is slightly compressed in the text.
items.plain_english: The salt ocean measures one hundred thousand yojanas. Outside it stand mountains, and to the north are Rishabha, Dundubhi, Dhumra, Kanka, Drona, and Indu.

rows.grounds: fire located between the two southern mountains

items.question: Which mountains stand to the west and south of the salt ocean, and what lies between the southern pair?
premises: Varaha, Nandana, Ashoka, and Balahaka stand in the west.
Chakra and Mainaka stand in the south.
The submarine fire is situated between Chakra and Mainaka.
items.inference: The salt ocean is surrounded by named mountains in different directions, with the submarine fire placed between the two southern mountains.
items.plain_english: To the west stand Varaha, Nandana, Ashoka, and Balahaka. To the south stand Chakra and Mainaka, and between those two is the submarine fire.

rows.grounds: name and dimensions of the mountain

items.question: What mountain lies south of the ocean and who lives there?
premises: South of the ocean, after a distance of two thousand yojanas, there is a mountain.
That mountain is named Vidyutvan and is three thousand yojanas high and wide.
Its inhabitants live on fruit.
items.inference: A large mountain named Vidyutvan lies south of the ocean and is inhabited by fruit-eating beings.
uncertainties: khākṣi is read as a numerical expression for two thousand.
items.plain_english: South of the ocean, two thousand yojanas away, stands the mountain Vidyutvan, three thousand yojanas high and wide. There live people who eat fruit.

rows.grounds: lifespan and diet of the inhabitants

items.question: How are the inhabitants of Vidyutvan described in appearance, conduct, and lifespan?
premises: The inhabitants are smeared with dirt, have long hair and beards, and go naked.
They have a cow-like nature.
They live for eighty years and eat grass.
items.inference: The people of Vidyutvan are portrayed as primitive, naked, grass-eating beings with a long but finite lifespan.
items.plain_english: They are smeared with dirt, have long hair and beards, go naked, and behave like cows. They live for eighty years and eat grass.

items.question: What scriptural authority describes the entrances to the netherworld in that region?
premises: There are always unbarred doors there for reaching the netherworld.
This teaching was sung by the teachers.
The teaching is found in the revered Raurava scripture.
items.inference: The account of open entrances to the netherworld is grounded in the authority of the Raurava scripture.
items.plain_english: There are always unbarred doors there for entering the netherworld. This is taught by the teachers in the revered Raurava scripture.

items.question: What lies beyond the salt ocean after its description is completed?
premises: The salt ocean has now been explained.
Beyond the salt ocean there are six continents.
Each of those continents is surrounded by its own ocean.
items.inference: The cosmography extends outward from the salt ocean into six further continents, each ringed by a distinct ocean.
items.plain_english: Thus the salt ocean has been described. Beyond it lie six continents, and each one is surrounded by its own ocean.

items.question: Which six continents and six oceans follow the salt ocean in order?
premises: The six continents are successively doubled in size and ruled by six sons of Manu.
The continents are Shaka, Kusha, Krauncha, Shalmali, Gomeda, and Pushkara.
The six oceans are of milk, curd, ghee, sugarcane juice, liquor, and sweet water.
items.inference: Beyond the salt ocean the world expands through six named continents and six corresponding oceans in a fixed order.
items.plain_english: The six continents, each successively doubled in size and ruled by six sons of Manu, are Shaka, Kusha, Krauncha, Shalmali, Gomeda, and Pushkara. Their six oceans are of milk, curd, ghee, sugarcane juice, liquor, and sweet water.

items.question: Who are the rulers assigned to Shaka and the other continents, and who rules Jambu?
premises: Medhatithi, Vapushmat, Jyotishmat, Dyutimat, King Havi, and Samvara rule Shaka and the other continents.
Agnidhra was appointed in Jambu continent.
items.inference: The cosmography assigns a specific Manu-descended ruler to each of the named continents, including Agnidhra for Jambu.
items.plain_english: Medhatithi, Vapushmat, Jyotishmat, Dyutimat, King Havi, and Samvara rule Shaka and the other continents, and Agnidhra was appointed over Jambu continent.

rows.gloss: Hari Yama Varuna and Indra there

items.question: How are Shaka and the other continents internally divided, and how is Pushkara arranged?
premises: The five continents beginning with Shaka are divided into regions by seven mountains each.
Pushkara is divided into two parts.
Hari, Yama, Varuna, and Indra rule there in the eastern and other directions.
items.inference: Most of the outer continents follow a seven-mountain division, while Pushkara has a distinct two-part structure with directional rulers.
uncertainties: The four rulers in Pushkara are given, but their exact assignment to the two parts is not fully explicit.
items.plain_english: The five continents beginning with Shaka are each divided into regions by seven mountains. Pushkara is divided into two parts, and there Hari, Yama, Varuna, and Indra rule in the east and the other directions.

rows.grounds: basis and unit of the measurement

items.question: What is the total measured extent from half of Meru to the end of the sweet-water ocean?
premises: The measurement is given in yojanas from half of Meru.
The extent reaches to the end of the sweet-water ocean.
The total measure is two crores, fifty-three hundred-thousands, and fifty thousand yojanas.
items.inference: The cosmography gives a precise cumulative distance for the world-system up to the sweet-water ocean.
uncertainties: The exact parsing of the large number compound follows the traditional reading but is compressed.
items.plain_english: From half of Meru up to the end of the sweet-water ocean, the total measure is two crores, fifty-three lakhs, and fifty thousand yojanas.

items.question: What lies beyond the seventh ocean and what boundary mountain is described there?
premises: Outside the seventh ocean there is a golden land extending ten crores of yojanas.
Beyond it is described the Lokāloka mountain, different from the inhabited world.
That mountain is one hundred thousand yojanas high and ten thousand yojanas broad.
items.inference: The golden land beyond the seventh ocean ends at the Lokāloka mountain, which marks the boundary of the world.
items.plain_english: Beyond the seventh ocean lies a golden land extending ten crores of yojanas. After that is the Lokāloka mountain, one hundred thousand yojanas high and ten thousand yojanas broad.

items.question: Who is stationed at Lokāloka and how far does the sun travel according to some teachers?
premises: A group of eight Rudras together with the world-lords is situated in the eight directions of Lokāloka.
Some teachers hold that the sun travels only within Lokāloka.
According to that view, the sun does not go beyond Lokāloka.
items.inference: Lokāloka is both a divine station of Rudras and, for some authorities, the outer limit of the sun's course.
items.plain_english: Eight Rudras with the world-lords are stationed in the eight directions of Lokāloka. Some say the sun moves only within Lokāloka and never goes beyond it.

items.question: How are the sun's northern and southern courses identified in traditional teaching?
premises: The paths of the ancestors and the gods go south and north.
These are described as two tracks beyond the sun's own rising point.
Teachers identify them as the sun's northern and southern courses.
items.inference: The traditional doctrine equates the ancestral and divine paths with the sun's two ayanas, its southern and northern courses.
uncertainties: The phrase svajātpare is somewhat compressed and may refer to the sun's position relative to its rising.
items.plain_english: The paths of the ancestors and the gods, going south and north, are the sun's two tracks. Teachers say these are the sun's southern and northern courses.

rows.grounds: how sunrise and sunset are understood

items.question: How should the sun's rising and setting be understood in relation to Meru and Lokāloka?
premises: Meru is said to be north of all.
Lokāloka is said to be south.
The sun's rising and setting should be conceived in relation to these two reference points.
items.inference: Sunrise and sunset are explained cosmographically by the fixed positions of Meru in the north and Lokāloka in the south.
items.plain_english: Meru is north of all and Lokāloka is south. In this way one should understand the sun's rising and setting.

items.question: How do the times of day differ simultaneously in the four directional cities?
premises: When it is midnight in Amaravati, it is sunset in Yama's city.
At that same time it is midday in Varuna's city.
At that same time it is sunrise in Soma's city.
items.inference: The sun's motion produces different simultaneous times in the four directional cities around Meru.
items.plain_english: When it is midnight in Amaravati, it is sunset in Yama's city, midday in Varuna's city, and sunrise in Soma's city.

items.question: How does the same solar motion create another set of simultaneous times in the four cities?
premises: When it is sunrise in Amaravati, it is midnight in Yama's abode.
At that same time it is sunset in Soma's city and midday in Varuna's city.
This pattern follows the sun's going and coming.
items.inference: The alternating times in the four cities are explained as effects of the sun's continuous circuit.
uncertainties: ke@staṃ is read as referring to Kubera/Soma's quarter with sunset.
items.plain_english: When it is sunrise in Amaravati, it is midnight in Yama's abode, sunset in Soma's city, and midday in Varuna's city. Thus the times change with the sun's movement.

items.question: How vast is the darkness beyond the Lokāloka mountain?
premises: Beyond the Lokāloka mountain there is darkness.
Its extent is measured in crores, lakhs, and thousands of yojanas.
The stated measure is thirty-five hundred crores, nineteen lakhs, and forty thousand yojanas.
items.inference: The cosmography places an immense region of darkness outside the boundary mountain of the world.
uncertainties: The large numerical compound is interpreted according to the standard cosmological reading.
items.plain_english: Beyond the Lokāloka mountain lies darkness extending thirty-five hundred crores, nineteen lakhs, and forty thousand yojanas.

items.question: What is the Garbhoda ocean and what does it contain beyond Lokāloka?
premises: Beyond Lokāloka lies the Garbhoda ocean, called the king of oceans.
Its measure is equal to that of the seven oceans.
The entire earth is contained within its womb.
items.inference: Garbhoda is presented as the vast containing ocean in which the whole earth-system rests.
items.plain_english: Beyond Lokāloka lies the Garbhoda ocean, the king of oceans, equal in measure to the seven oceans. In its womb rests the entire earth.

items.question: What does the Siddhanta scripture place on the shore of the Garbhoda ocean?
premises: The Siddhanta scripture describes a region on the shore of the Garbhoda ocean.
That region is named Kausheya.
Garuda dwells there surrounded by accomplished birds.
items.inference: The shore of the Garbhoda ocean contains a named region, Kausheya, associated with Garuda and his retinue.
items.plain_english: According to the Siddhanta scripture, on the shore of the Garbhoda ocean is a region called Kausheya. There Garuda lives surrounded by accomplished birds.

items.question: What features are found in the Kausheya region beyond Garuda's presence?
premises: Beings sport on the mountain tops there.
There are nine principal mountains in that region.
Beyond them flow thirty hot-water rivers that go down to the netherworld.
items.inference: The Kausheya region contains inhabited mountain heights and a system of hot rivers descending to the netherworld.
uncertainties: The compound at the end is dense and may also imply a sequence of locations.
items.plain_english: There they sport on mountain tops, and there are nine principal mountains. Beyond them are thirty hot-water rivers that flow down to the netherworld.

items.question: What sequence of regions and beings follows the hot-water rivers toward the cosmic enclosure?
premises: There is the Naimi garden in the four directions, always attended by yoginis.
Beyond it come Meru, then serpents, then clouds.
After that comes the golden egg.
items.inference: The cosmography moves through a sacred sequence from the yogini-attended garden to the golden cosmic enclosure.
uncertainties: The brief list may compress distinct regions into a single sequence.
items.plain_english: Then comes the Naimi garden in the four directions, always attended by yoginis. After that are Meru, the serpents, the clouds, and then the golden egg.

items.question: What is the total extent of the world called Bhurloka within Brahma's cosmic shell?
premises: The world is bounded by the shell of Brahma's egg.
Its extent is measured in relation to half of Meru.
It extends fifty crores of yojanas in the ten directions and is called Bhurloka.
items.inference: Bhurloka is defined as a vast, directionally measured world enclosed within Brahma's cosmic egg.
uncertainties: The role of merorardhena in the measurement is syntactically compressed.
items.plain_english: Enclosed by the shell of Brahma's egg, the world called Bhurloka extends fifty crores of yojanas in the ten directions.

items.question: Which kinds of beings pervade the earth-world called Bhurloka?
premises: Bhurloka is pervaded by six classes: beasts, birds, deer, trees, humans, and reptiles.
It is also inhabited by pishachas, rakshasas, gandharvas, and yakshas.
items.inference: Bhurloka contains both ordinary embodied life-forms and various semi-divine or supernatural beings.
items.plain_english: This earth-world is filled with six kinds of beings: beasts, birds, deer, trees, humans, and reptiles. It is also inhabited by pishachas, rakshasas, gandharvas, and yakshas.

items.question: How broadly does Bhurloka serve as a place of enjoyment and residence for beings?
premises: Vidyadharas and many other beings are included in Bhurloka.
The text extends the account to the whole creation of beings.
All beings may have places of enjoyment and residence there according to their desire.
items.inference: Bhurloka functions as a comprehensive world of habitation and enjoyment for the full range of embodied beings.
uncertainties: abhimānato can suggest desire, self-conception, or inclination; 'according to desire' fits the context best.
items.plain_english: It is also the abode of vidyadharas, and in short, for the whole creation of beings it serves as a place of enjoyment and residence according to their desire.
